title: Cost and Resource Optimization on Google Cloud
bodyMarkdown:
## Why this matters for the PCA exam

Cost optimization is where technical and business processes meet. Scenarios describe a steady baseline, a bursty tier and some batch jobs, then ask which pricing mechanism fits each, or they describe a surprise bill and ask what governance would have caught it. You are expected to know the pricing levers, the tools that surface waste, the guardrails that notify rather than stop, and how to frame the financial model for executives. The Well-Architected Framework [cost optimization pillar](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/cost-optimization) summarizes the posture in four principles: align cloud spending with business value, foster a culture of cost awareness, optimize resource usage, and optimize continuously.

## Where cost sits in the Well-Architected Framework

The [Well-Architected Framework](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/framework) has six pillars: operational excellence, security, privacy and compliance, reliability, cost optimization, performance optimization, and sustainability. It builds on a design foundation of five principles: design for change, document your architecture, simplify design and use fully managed services, decouple your architecture, and use a stateless architecture. Pillars trade off against each other, so an exam answer that maximizes one pillar blindly (for example hot multi-region everything for reliability) is usually the distractor. Choose the option that meets the stated requirements and no more. Cross-pillar perspectives exist for AI and ML workloads and for financial services.

The sustainability pillar has a concrete tool. [Carbon Footprint](https://docs.cloud.google.com/carbon-footprint/docs/export) reports emissions for your Google Cloud usage in the console and exports it through BigQuery Data Transfer Service to a monthly partitioned `carbon_footprint` table, with each month's data exported on the 15th of the following month and a backfill reaching back to January 2021. It reports scope 2 on both location-based and market-based methods. Use it to measure, then act on the same Active Assist recommendations used for cost (idle resources, rightsizing); sustainability and cost usually move together.

## CapEx versus OpEx

Capital expenditure (CapEx) is large upfront spending on hardware and data centers, depreciated over years, and forces you to forecast peak capacity and over-provision. Operating expenditure (OpEx) is pay-for-consumption. Moving to Google Cloud shifts spend from CapEx toward OpEx, which improves cash flow and ties cost to usage. The trade-off is that nobody is forced to justify a purchase order, so waste accumulates unless you add governance. Answers claiming the cloud "eliminates costs" or "has no effect on the financial model" are wrong.

## Compute pricing levers

| Mechanism | Commitment | Discount | Best for | Watch out |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| On-demand | None | None | Spiky, short-lived, unknown demand | Highest unit price |
| Sustained use discounts (SUDs) | None, automatic | Up to 30% or 20% depending on series | Steady usage on eligible older series | Many newer series are not listed as eligible |
| Committed use discounts (CUDs) | 1 or 3 years | Deeper than SUDs | Stable, predictable baseline | You pay the commitment whether you use it or not |
| Spot VMs | None | Up to 91% | Fault-tolerant, interruptible batch and stateless work | No SLA, can be preempted at any time |

### Sustained use discounts

Per the [SUD documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/sustained-use-discounts), Compute Engine applies them automatically. Eligible resources include vCPUs and memory of N1, N2 and N2D machine types, C2, and M1 and M2, plus shared-core types and sole-tenant nodes. Discounts reach up to 30% for N1, M1, M2 and shared-core types and up to 20% for N2, N2D and C2. They accrue in steps as usage covers more of the month. Resources covered by CUDs are not eligible. The page lists specific older series and does not list newer ones such as E2, so do not assume a SUD applies to every VM. When a question says SUDs "apply automatically," it is describing the mechanism; when a scenario depends on the number, check the series.

### Committed use discounts

The [CUD overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/docs/cuds) distinguishes two families, both with one-year or three-year terms:

- **Resource-based CUDs** commit to vCPU, memory, GPU and Local SSD amounts, are Compute Engine only, and apply to a specific region.
- **Spend-based CUDs** commit to a dollar amount per hour of eligible spend, purchased at the billing account level, and apply across linked projects and across regions. Covered services include Cloud SQL, Spanner, BigQuery, Bigtable, AlloyDB, Memorystore, Dataflow and Firestore, and Compute Engine, Cloud Run and GKE via flexible commitments.

The [Compute Engine CUD comparison](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/committed-use-discounts-overview) shows the trade-off. At the time of review, compute flexible CUDs list 28% for one year and 46% for three years on general-purpose families, apply across machine series, projects and regions within the billing account, and cover E2 and N1 to N4 among others. Resource-based CUDs list up to 55% on general-purpose hardware but are tied to the region and project. Both types cannot be cancelled after purchase. Discount tables change, so treat the percentages as a snapshot and the structure as the lasting lesson.

Rule of thumb: stable 24/7 baseline with no wish to lock into a machine shape or region means **flexible (spend-based) CUDs**. A fixed shape in a fixed region that will not change means resource-based. Also remember that you are billed a monthly fee for the commitment regardless of use for the entire commitment period, so over-committing to peak is a classic error.

### Spot VMs

[Spot VMs](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/spot) offer up to 91% off for machine types, GPUs, TPUs and Local SSDs. They use excess capacity, so availability varies, they are excluded from the Compute Engine SLA, and they can be preempted. By default a preempted VM is stopped, but you can choose delete. There is no enforced maximum runtime unless you configure one. Use them for batch, rendering, CI workers and stateless tiers that checkpoint or retry. Never use them for the always-on baseline or anything that cannot tolerate interruption.

### Matching tiers to levers

For the classic three-tier scenario the answer is: commit to the steady baseline, autoscale the fluctuating tier on on-demand, and run the nightly fault-tolerant batch on Spot. Putting everything on three-year CUDs sized to peak pays for unused capacity; putting everything on Spot risks outages; staying on-demand forfeits the baseline discount.

## Finding and removing waste

- **Active Assist and Recommender.** [Active Assist](https://docs.cloud.google.com/recommender/docs/whatis-activeassist) generates recommendations across six categories: cost, performance, security, reliability, sustainability and manageability. Cost-related examples include VM rightsizing, idle VM, idle disk and idle IP address recommendations, and CUD recommendations. Surfaces include the Active Assist dashboard, FinOps Hub for billing account managers, in-context console views, the API and the gcloud CLI. Google advises a reviewer in your organization to assess impact before applying a recommendation, so recommendations are inputs to a change process, not auto-apply buttons.
- **Schedule non-production.** [Instance schedules](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/schedule-instance-start-stop) are resource policies that start and stop VMs. Limits: up to 1,000 VMs per schedule, one schedule per VM, operations can lag up to 15 minutes, and you cannot stop instances that have Local SSD disks with a schedule.
- **Tier storage.** [Cloud Storage classes](https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/storage-classes) are Standard (no minimum duration), Nearline (30 days, about monthly access), Coldline (90 days, about quarterly) and Archive (365 days, less than yearly). Colder classes have retrieval fees and minimum storage durations, so moving hot data to Archive can cost more. All classes support Autoclass for automatic transitions.
- **Autoscale and use scale-to-zero platforms.** Cloud Run removes instances when there are no requests and can bill by request or by instance lifetime; GKE Autopilot bills general-purpose Pods by their resource requests.

## Visibility and governance

### Budgets and alerts

A [Cloud Billing budget](https://docs.cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/budgets) defaults to alert thresholds of 50%, 90% and 100% of the budget amount, calculated on actual spend, with options to alert on forecasted spend. Scope can be the whole billing account or specific projects, services, labels or folders. Email goes to billing admins and users by default; Pub/Sub enables programmatic responses.

The critical exam fact: an alerts-only budget does not automatically cap usage or spending. The [programmatic notification guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/notify) adds the caveats: messages arrive multiple times per day, the first one may take several hours, Pub/Sub delivery is at-least-once and can arrive out of order, so costs may overshoot before an automated response runs. Google documents disabling billing via notification as one possible response, but that is a design you own, with the delay and overshoot just described. A spend cap budget is a preview feature for eligible services.

### Billing export and labels

[Billing export to BigQuery](https://docs.cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/export-data-bigquery) offers standard usage cost, detailed usage cost (resource-level), pricing data and CUD metadata (preview). Labels appear in the exports, so consistent labels by team, environment and application are what make showback and chargeback possible. Enable export early: regional datasets only collect data from the day you enable them, while multi-region EU or US datasets backfill from the start of the previous month.

## A practical optimization order

1. Eliminate idle resources and schedule non-production: highest return, lowest risk.
2. Rightsize using Recommender data, after review.
3. Tier storage and tune autoscaling.
4. Commit with CUDs only on the stable, understood baseline.
5. Run Spot for interruptible work.
6. Make it continuous: budgets, labels, billing export and regular cost reviews.

## Anti-patterns and common mistakes

- **Committing before rightsizing.** You lock in a three-year commitment for oversized VMs.
- **Committing to peak.** Commitments should cover the floor, not the ceiling.
- **Treating budgets as hard caps.** They notify; any shutdown automation is yours to build and has latency.
- **Spot for the baseline.** Cheap until the preemption lands during peak.
- **Archive for data read monthly.** Retrieval fees and the 365 day minimum exceed the savings.
- **No labels.** Without them cost allocation is guesswork.
- **Optimizing one pillar in isolation.** Cutting cost by removing redundancy, or maximizing reliability with unneeded active-active, ignores the framework's trade-offs.
- **Cost reviews done once.** Optimization is continuous: usage drifts, recommendations refresh and discount structures change.
- **Applying recommendations blindly.** A rightsizing suggestion based on an average can break a monthly spike.

## Exam tips

- **Stable baseline plus no machine-type lock-in:** flexible (spend-based) CUDs. **Fixed shape in a fixed region:** resource-based CUDs. **Interruptible batch:** Spot. **Spiky:** on-demand with autoscaling.
- **Three-tier answer:** commit the baseline, autoscale the variable tier, Spot for fault-tolerant batch. Reject "everything on Spot" and "everything on three-year CUDs sized to peak."
- **Budgets alert, they do not cap.** Pub/Sub notifications connect to automation, with delay and possible overshoot. Default thresholds are 50%, 90% and 100%.
- **Rightsizing and idle detection:** Active Assist Recommender. Cloud Trace measures request latency; it does not recommend machine sizes.
- **CapEx to OpEx:** the cloud shifts upfront capital spending to consumption-based operating spending and requires governance.
- **Order of operations:** remove idle, rightsize, then commit.
- **Storage:** match class to access frequency and watch minimum durations of 30, 90 and 365 days.
- **Well-Architected Framework:** six pillars (operational excellence, security, reliability, cost optimization, performance optimization, sustainability); pick the design that meets requirements, not the maximum of one pillar. Carbon Footprint is the emissions reporting tool, exported to BigQuery.
- **Showback and chargeback** need labels plus BigQuery billing export.

diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  Start["Workload usage profile"] --> Q1{"Interruptible and fault tolerant?"}
  Q1 -->|"Yes"| Spot["Spot VMs"]
  Q1 -->|"No"| Q2{"Stable 24/7 baseline?"}
  Q2 -->|"Yes, shape may change"| Flex["Flexible spend-based CUDs"]
  Q2 -->|"Yes, fixed shape and region"| Res["Resource-based CUDs"]
  Q2 -->|"No"| OnD["On-demand with autoscaling"]
  Flex --> Right["Rightsize first with Recommender"]
  Res --> Right
  OnD --> Right
  Right --> Gov["Budgets, labels and billing export"]

diagrams.title: Budget alert automation path
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  Spend["Spend crosses 50, 90 or 100 percent"] --> Bud["Cloud Billing budget"]
  Bud --> Mail["Email to billing admins"]
  Bud --> PS["Pub/Sub topic"]
  PS --> Auto["Your automation, for example notify or scale down"]
  Auto --> Note["Delayed and can overshoot: budget is not a hard cap"]
